title: Results by year, against the State and ten like districts
question: While spending per pupil rose, what happened to test results, attendance and graduation?
finding: The share of San Francisco pupils meeting the State standard in English was 56.5% in 2018-19 and 53.5% in 2025-26 (State: 51.1% to 49.3%); in mathematics 50.5% and 45.8% (State: 39.7% to 38.4%). Its rank among the eleven districts went from 2 to 3 in English and 1 to 2 in mathematics. Chronic absenteeism was 18.8% in 2018-19 and 28.8% in 2024-25 (State 19.4%; rank 8 of 11, 1 = least absence). Four-year graduation at regular schools was 87.3% against 92.1% statewide.
how: State-published district figures for all pupils: the share meeting or exceeding the standard on the State tests in grades 3 to 8 and 11; the share of pupils absent for a tenth or more of the days they were enrolled; and the four-year graduation rate. Rank 1 is the best of the eleven districts (highest for tests and graduation, lowest for absence). Graduation is shown for regular schools, with the all-schools figure beside it: the all-schools rate for San Francisco is pulled far down because the district row includes a large charter school for adults and people in custody that the district authorised.
limits: Spending and results are linked by many things besides management: who the pupils are, how many are learning English or are poor, the pandemic and the length of school closures, and which families chose private or charter schools. A district-wide average hides differences between schools and groups of pupils. Test rows cover the district's own schools; absence and graduation rows include charter schools it authorised. A district where living costs are high must pay more to hire and keep staff, and one with many small schools, or with many pupils who are learning English, have disabilities or are poor, will spend more per pupil for honest reasons; none of those is measured here.
